name: ACE

paper.title: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models

construction.unit: bullet: id, helpful/harmful counters, one short strategy, concept, formula, code snippet or failure mode, filed under a section
construction.kept_as: LLM-written lessons (Reflector diagnoses, Curator phrases the bullet)
construction.processing: Generator answers with the playbook; Reflector diagnoses the attempt against feedback and tags used bullets; Curator proposes new bullets as ADD operations
construction.writer: the same LLM in three roles (DeepSeek-V3.1 non-thinking by default)

organization.structure: one playbook of bullets grouped under fixed section headings
organization.stores: a single text playbook (the context) per task domain

management.operations: deterministic append of Curator ADDs under their section with fresh ids; helpful/harmful counters incremented from Reflector tags; optional embedding dedup with LLM merge (off by default in code)
management.conflicts: not resolved in code: UPDATE, MERGE and DELETE are listed as TODO
management.forgetting: paper: lazy pruning when the context window is exceeded; not in the released code

retrieval.candidates: none: the whole playbook is read
retrieval.selection: none; the Generator lists the ids of bullets it found useful
retrieval.budget: whole playbook (curator prompt states an 80k-token budget but nothing enforces it)

use.context: full playbook plus question and context (finance); playbook inside the first ReAct prompt, before the task (AppWorld)
use.reasoning: single JSON answer (finance) or ReAct loop up to 40 steps (AppWorld)

classify.note: Sections are headings inside one prompt, not separate stores. Counters change in place, but bullet text is only ever added in the released code; the paper's de-duplication is an optional flag.

stages.ingestion: Each training sample (offline, up to 5 epochs) or each test sample (online) is answered by the Generator with the current playbook; its reasoning, answer and the ids of bullets it used are kept.
stages.construction: The Reflector compares the attempt with feedback (ground-truth answer, or execution result / unit tests on AppWorld), explains the error, and tags used bullets helpful or harmful; if the answer was wrong it can refine over several rounds while the Generator retries. The Curator then writes only new bullets as ADD operations.
stages.organization: One playbook of bullets under fixed section headings (e.g. strategies, formulas, code snippets, common mistakes); each bullet has an id and helpful/harmful counters.
stages.update: Non-LLM merge: ADDs get fresh ids and are appended under their section; counters are incremented from the Reflector's tags. The paper adds embedding-based de-duplication and lazy pruning (grow-and-refine); in the code dedup is an optional flag and pruning is absent.
stages.retrieval: None. The whole playbook is placed in every Generator call; the Generator reports which bullet ids it relied on.
stages.answer: Generator answers with the full playbook, the question and its context (finance), or acts in AppWorld's ReAct loop with the playbook in its system prompt.

summary: Treats the prompt as a growing playbook of itemised bullets: a Generator uses it, a Reflector diagnoses each attempt against feedback and scores bullets, and a Curator appends new bullets as small deltas merged without an LLM, avoiding the collapse that full LLM rewrites cause.

headline: There is no retrieval: every bullet in the playbook goes into every call, so the context grows with experience (24.9k vs 10.9k input tokens per AppWorld call against GEPA).
The Curator only adds; the released code implements ADD alone, so bullets are never rewritten or deleted and de-duplication is an optional switch.

paper_vs_code.code: only ADD is implemented (UPDATE/MERGE/DELETE are TODO); dedup is an opt-in flag (off by default, none in the sequential AppWorld agent); no pruning; the token budget is only text in the Curator prompt

paper_vs_code.paper: each test sample is predicted with the current context, then used to update it
paper_vs_code.code: finance code scores a whole window (15 samples by default) with the playbook from before the window, then trains on each sample

open_questions: How much of the gain comes from simply having a long, detailed prompt rather than from what the reflect-curate loop writes? No run gives the Generator an equally long playbook written without feedback.
Because every bullet is always read, the method's cost and noise grow with the playbook; the paper's pruning study (Table 21) is on FiNER only and its pruning is not in the released code.

components.model: DeepSeek-V3.1, non-thinking (also GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1, Llama-3.3-70B in App. A.1)

discussion.takeaway: Letting a context grow as an itemised playbook, written by reflection and merged in small deltas rather than rewritten, beats prompt optimisers and Dynamic Cheatsheet on AppWorld and financial tasks, at lower adaptation cost.

claims.evidence: AppWorld average 59.4 offline and 59.5 online vs ReAct 42.4, GEPA 46.4, DC 51.9 (DeepSeek-V3.1). Table 1
FiNER/Formula average 81.9 offline vs GEPA 72.5 and base 69.1. Table 2

claims.claim: Works without labels when execution feedback exists.
claims.evidence: AppWorld offline without labels 57.2 vs 59.4 with; but finance online without labels drops to 67.3 on FiNER (base 70.7). Tables 1-2

claims.claim: Full rewriting collapses contexts; deltas avoid it.
claims.evidence: DC context fell from 18,282 to 122 tokens and 66.7 → 57.1; removing incremental updates cuts test-normal TGC 76.2 → 67.3. §2.2, Table 18
−82.3% latency and −75.1% rollouts vs GEPA offline; −91.5% latency and −83.6% token cost vs DC online. Table 4
Gains with GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1 and Llama-3.3-70B. Tables 5-9

limits: Depends on a reasonably strong Reflector; poor insights make the context noisy or harmful.
Without reliable feedback (labels or execution signals) adaptation can hurt.
Not every task needs a long context; tasks like HotPotQA or Game of 24 gain little.
reading: There is no retrieval: every call carries the whole playbook, which on AppWorld more than doubles input tokens per call (Table 15); the paper argues KV-cache reuse offsets the cost.

The released code only appends bullets; UPDATE/MERGE/DELETE are TODO, dedup is off by default and pruning is not implemented, so the 'refine' half of grow-and-refine is not what the code runs by default.
Table 1's online ACE row (59.5) is the warm-started variant from Table 3; the plain online run is 56.1, still above DC (51.9), which gets no warm-up.
'Without labels' on finance still gives the Reflector a right/wrong signal in the released code; on AppWorld it means execution output instead of ground-truth code and unit tests.
The offline finance run keeps the playbook with the best validation accuracy, so validation labels steer the no-label rows too; the released test files are subsets (FiNER 441, Formula 200 questions).
All three roles use the same model, so gains are not from a stronger teacher (§4.2); Table 16 shows a weaker Reflector still helps.

abstract.text: ACE improves an LLM application by editing its context instead of its weights. The context is a playbook of small, itemised bullets that grows over time: a Generator attempts tasks, a Reflector turns successes and failures into lessons, and a Curator adds new bullets that are merged by simple code rather than rewritten by an LLM. The authors argue this avoids brevity bias and the 'context collapse' seen when an LLM repeatedly rewrites its whole context. On AppWorld and financial reasoning benchmarks it beats prompt optimisers and Dynamic Cheatsheet in both offline and online adaptation, with lower adaptation latency and cost.
